newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - LME reforms continue, more information freed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - LME reforms continue, more information freed.

text.p: The pace of change on the London Metal Exchange (LME) following 1996's multi-billion dollar Sumitomo Corp copper scandal continues, with formerly sensitive market data becoming more transparent.
On Wednesday the LME said it would release data on warehouse inventory levels on a daily basis from April 7. At present, LME stock changes are reported only twice a week.
"I think that this will be a useful step...the transparancy of stock movements will be increased," an industry source said.
It will make stock movement intelligence more speedily available and also limit the impact of the announcement as a market factor, he said.

But some traders were less enthusiastic about the measure - the latest in a string of reforms that followed a review of the LME by Britain's top regulator the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) last December.
"It has been done to appease the regulators. Twice-weekly, you get a bit of excitement. Reported daily, it loses the impact and that is not good for the market-place," one LME trader said.

Others said the LME was treading a fine line in opening up information on stocks, ownership of the metal, large market positions and information-sharing, while attempting not to reduce commercial trading opportunities.

Since January the LME has been introducing a range of measures recommended by the SIB last December. The review was called for by the LME following June's Sumitomo bombshell, when the Japanese company announced losses of $2.6 billion incurred during 10 years of unauthorised copper trading carried out by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
Last week and also this week, there have been meetings of the LME sub-committees charged with implementing SIB recommendations.

These have been exploring ways of releasing data on the size and nature of large long and short positions in the market, as well as ownership of warrants - the documents showing title to warehouse stocks.
"There are practical difficulties and technical issues that need to be discussed as to who actually owns the metal," the industry source said.
Banks, for instance, control and finance significant tonnages of metal, but they may not ultimately own the stockpile.
Regarding market positions, there may be a blur between what is classed as trade business or speculative involvement.
However, the LME is already receiving information on large positions, and it may be conceivable to make public the concentration of open interest on certain dates, trade sources said.

"There is a trade-off...you can't have all the cards on the table. But we think that the LME is moving in the right direction, and would not like to see the impetus of the SIB review lost," the industry source said.
